items.title: Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a...
items.content:
Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out.

It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend.

The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans).

More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains.

In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries.

Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology.

I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out.

items.title: Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside...
items.content:
Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR.

We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use.

Read more: https://t.co/RuEosScSMb

items.title: The Intelligence Index vs Cost per Task Pareto frontier shifted this week with the releases of MiMo-...
items.content:
The Intelligence Index vs Cost per Task Pareto frontier shifted this week with the releases of MiMo-V2.6-Pro, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6 Sol

Together they have established eleven new points on the Pareto frontier (driven by different reasoning efforts): five from GPT-6 Luna, one each from MiMo-V2.6-Pro and GPT-6 Sol, and four from Claude Opus 5.5.

GPT-6 Luna (max) scores 37 at $0.068 per task, MiMo-V2.6-Pro scores 46 at $0.13, GPT-6 Sol (max) scores 48 at $1.06, and Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) is the new highest-scoring model at 58 at $5.98.

Full transcript:

Minister Barrot, members of the Security Council, thank you for the invitation. As...
items.content:
Full transcript:

Minister Barrot, members of the Security Council, thank you for the invitation. As a French national who moved to the US 15 years ago, with a Brazilian wife and two American daughters, I sometimes feel like I’m practicing international collaboration on a daily basis, which gives me a particular appreciation for the challenging work you’re all doing here.

I’m also the cofounder and CEO of Hugging Face. We’re lucky to be one of the most widely used platforms for developers and agents building AI based on open-source models and datasets. This July, we became the first company to publicly disclose an autonomous agent cyberattack to the world, and today I want to share three critical lessons from it.

First, we need much more transparency in AI. I often wonder what would have happened if we had decided not to disclose the attack publicly. Especially now that we know similar incidents had been happening months earlier in secret at a handful of frontier labs without monitoring. To better understand and mitigate these emerging cybersecurity risks, the global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure. For example through mandatory sharing of full agent traces. We learned this summer that building and keeping some of these systems behind closed doors is not safe.

Second, we learned that the biggest risk is not simply powerful AI. It is the asymmetry of powerful AI. Asymmetry between attackers and defenders. Between a few companies and everyone else. Between a few countries and the rest of the world. Asymmetry of control, of capabilities, of compute, of power. When we got attacked, our team initially turned to frontier closed-source APIs that blocked us because of safeguards that still can’t always tell the difference between attackers and defenders. I acknowledge that these safeguards are created with good intentions, but they can put defenders at a disadvantage while attackers jailbreak them, increasing the asymmetry of capabilities. In our case, as we started hitting those guardrails, fortunately we could use the NVIDIA version of an open-source model coming from China called GLM 5.2 by https://t.co/XE7H9L1vKE, and we’re very grateful for that. It reinforced our conviction about the importance of open-source AI. Cyberattacks may increasingly come from proprietary models behind closed doors, while much of the defense may end up being powered by open-source tools because they are less restricted, more privacy-preserving, and orders of magnitude more affordable for organizations across the globe. The world needs open-source AI more than ever to defend itself. This applies not only to cybersecurity but to AI in general, where there has never been a greater need to distribute capabilities, resources, and control rather than concentrate them in the hands of a few. 

Third, during this cyberattack, we learned how AI can stoke fear among the public and policymakers, especially through anthropomorphic framing and sci-fi imagery. We strongly believe that fear-based narratives are not the way to make the right decisions about the future of such a foundational and empowering technology or bring the public along with us. Even though we were the victims of this cyberattack, we believe more strongly than ever that AI will be beneficial to cybersecurity and make the world safer, just as major technologies before it. We were attacked by AI, but more importantly, we defended ourselves with AI. The same systems that helped us during this attack are now helping us against cyberattacks we were already facing. AI is also helping us fix the bugs and weaknesses in our systems before any attack, the same way AI is helping OAI fix their sandboxes to prevent agents from escaping. AI won't just create new cybersecurity challenges. It can make cybersecurity fundamentally and meaningfully stronger if we keep the right incentives, equip defenders more than attackers, and don’t increase the asymmetry between them. And that's before considering AI's positive impact on science, healthcare, education, productivity, and much more. 

In closing, I want to reiterate what this first agent cyberattack taught us: the need for more transparency in AI and more open-source AI to fight asymmetry empower defenders and countries big and small. Thank you again to the UN Security Council and Minister Barrot for inviting me to speak today. The Hugging Face team, community and myself are at your disposal.

items.title: We’ve run the most comprehensive series of studies on expert AI forecasts over the last four years. ...
items.content:
We’ve run the most comprehensive series of studies on expert AI forecasts over the last four years. Today, we’re sharing an interim update on our findings about the accuracy of these forecasts.

Our major findings are:

1. Experts, including top economists, computer scientists, and biologists, have dramatically underestimated AI capabilities progress each year. Superforecasters have underestimated progress to an even greater extent.

2. Experts have a more mixed forecasting track record on AI diffusion-related measures, with some major underestimates (forecasting AI revenue) and other forecasts on track to be accurate (the share of electricity used for AI).

3. Some notable cases of overestimating AI progress: how much mid-2025 AI models could help amateurs do biorisk-relevant laboratory tasks; the speed of rollout of self-driving cars.

4. It is too soon to say how forecasters have performed at predicting macro-scale impact on outcomes such as GDP growth, major AI harms, and averted deaths from disease.

More details for the formal methods people -- what's happening is Claude is doing something like:

1. Building a model of the program, targeting a tricky state machine or race-prone part of the code
2. Finding counter-examples in the model. These are suspected bugs
3. Reproducing the bugs
4. Fixing the bugs in the code

It's not that the whole codebase is formally verified (yet!..), more that the hairiest parts of the code are modeled, checked for counter-examples, and fixed.

items.title: PosteriorBench: going beyond point reconstructions for  scientific inverse-problem to full posterior...
items.content:
PosteriorBench: going beyond point reconstructions for  scientific inverse-problem to full posterior distributions.

Many scientific problems involve indirect or partial observations. Multiple physical fields can explain the same measurements. A solver should capture these possibilities, yet reconstruction accuracy alone is misleading.

We spent substantial compute to construct high-fidelity reference posteriors across four tasks: Darcy flow inversion, Poisson source recovery, carbon capture and storage, and light transport material inference. These reference data let researchers directly evaluate their solvers using five complementary metrics.

One of our key findings: better reconstruction accuracy can coincide with worse posterior recovery. Even strong generative samplers struggle to get both the mean and variance right, often underestimating the uncertainty.

Paper: https://t.co/klzMrIbLJB
Code: https://t.co/wPBBzcP5V2

Thanks to Jiachen Yao, Sean Hsu, Xi Deng, and all our coauthors for making this work possible @Caltech 

#AIforScience #InverseProblems #UncertaintyQuantification

This is the first result from our new molecular biology lab, where a team of Anthropic biologists is using Claude to explore and accelerate fundamental biology research. There, Claude works through data and literature to generate hypotheses and candidate biological systems to study. After our scientists review Claude’s hypotheses, they test the most promising ideas, with all lab work done by our scientists.

We’d like to extend this approach to a broad range of problems—in genomics and in other fields. If you have a proposal for a research question, we’d like to hear from you.

We first found evidence of this in our Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT). We collected forecasts in mid-2022 and followed up on results in mid-2025.

Most forecasters greatly underestimated AI progress across three benchmarks (MATH, MMLU, and QuALITY) by mid-2024 and were particularly surprised by AI achieving International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) gold-level performance in July 2025. The IMO milestone happened five years earlier than the median expert prediction and 10 years earlier than the median superforecaster prediction.

These forecasts were collected prior to the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. We wondered if forecasters would similarly underestimate AI progress post-ChatGPT.

Most forecasters greatly underestimated AI progress across three benchmarks (MATH, MMLU, and QuALITY) by mid-2024 and were particularly surprised by AI achieving International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) gold-level performance in July 2025. The IMO milestone happened five years earlier than the median expert prediction and 10 years earlier than the median superforecaster prediction.

These forecasts were collected prior to the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. We wondered if forecasters would similarly underestimate AI progress post-ChatGPT.

items.title: Google has released Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS. Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS debuts ...
items.content:
Google has released Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS. Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS debuts at #1 on our Pronunciation Robustness Benchmark and #2 on our Provider Voice Arena Leaderboard

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are @GoogleDeepMind's latest Text to Speech models, supporting preset voices and voice replication. Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS led our Pronunciation Robustness Benchmark at launch, with Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS now taking the top spot and scoring 64 Elo points higher in our Provider Voice Arena.

Key takeaways:

➤ #2 in Provider Voice Arena: Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS debuts at #2 with an Elo of 1,263, just behind Sonic 3.6 at 1,272 and ahead of Qwen-Audio-3.0-TTS-Plus at 1,260. Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS debuts at #6 with an Elo of 1,236, just 1 point behind Simba 3.2. Both models rank ahead of Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS at 1,199.

➤ #1 in Pronunciation Robustness: Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS takes #1 at 89.5%, ahead of Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS at 88.2%, SpaceXAI TTS at 87.6%, and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS at 87.4%, placing three Google models in the top four.

➤ Multilingual: Across our 9 multilingual Controlled Voice Arenas, Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS debuts at #1 in Japanese, #2 in Arabic, and #3 in German. Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS ranks #2 in Japanese and Portuguese.

➤ Speed: Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS processes 44.1 characters per second, compared to 40.2 characters per second for Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS, approximately 2.7x and 2.4x faster than realtime, respectively.

➤ Pricing: Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS is priced at $32.98/1M characters, compared to $22.07/1M characters for Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS. Both are more expensive than Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS at $18.31/1M characters, but substantially cheaper than Eleven v3 at $100/1M characters.

See below for more details  ⬇️

items.title: Forecasters also underestimated AI progress on some non-benchmark indicators such as revenue growth ...
items.content:
Forecasters also underestimated AI progress on some non-benchmark indicators such as revenue growth for top AI companies.

In late 2025 to early 2026, we ran a study asking economists, AI experts, and superforecasters to forecast a variety of impacts that AI could have on the economy.

An early economic indicator we asked them to forecast was the highest annual recurring revenue (ARR) for an AI-focused company at the end of 2026. Economists gave a median ARR of $16 billion, AI experts predicted $20 billion, and superforecasters predicted $25 billion.

As of late July, best-guess estimates were that Anthropic had achieved an ARR of $65 billion, indicating that forecasters are on track to significantly underestimate revenue growth. (More recent reporting suggests Anthropic is on track to reach $100 billion ARR by the end of 2026.)

Finally, and most recently, we have seen that forecasters in our Longitudinal Expert AI Panel underestimated how quickly AI would assist with solving a Millennium Prize Problem.

In August–September 2025, the median AI expert in our sample gave just a 10% chance of AI solving a Millennium Prize Problem by the end of 2027, while the median superforecaster gave even lower odds of 5.4%.

Although official resolution of this question will require more definitive communication from the Clay Mathematics Institute, which may take some time, it seems clear that forecasters did not expect this degree of progress this quickly.

items.title:
We don't talk enough about this, but the database we've always known is dead.

Modern applications n...
items.content:
We don't talk enough about this, but the database we've always known is dead.

Modern applications need to store structured data, JSON documents, relationships, vector embeddings, spatial data, and text.

So far, the solution most people use is to break the data across different systems:

• Relational data goes to the RDBMS
• Embeddings go to a vector database
• JSON documents go to a NoSQL database

Trust me, this is a nightmare.

You don't want to synchronize updates and coordinate failures across all these systems.

The solution: "Converged Databases".

Here is how a converged database works:

1. You can save related changes in a single transaction. Every change either succeeds or fails.

2. Your queries can combine relational data, JSON documents, and vectors.

3. All changes across your data stay in sync at all times. You don’t need to wait for them to catch up.

4. Your permissions work regardless of how you search the data and the fields you retrieve.

5. You can work with different views of the same data. For example, you can return customer data as a JSON document or relational data.

items.content_html:
We don't talk enough about this, but the database we've always known is dead.

Modern applications need to store structured data, JSON documents, relationships, vector embeddings, spatial data, and text.

So far, the solution most people use is to break the data across different systems:

• Relational data goes to the RDBMS

• Embeddings go to a vector database

• JSON documents go to a NoSQL database

Trust me, this is a nightmare.

You don't want to synchronize updates and coordinate failures across all these systems.

The solution: "Converged Databases".

Here is how a converged database works:

1. You can save related changes in a single transaction. Every change either succeeds or fails.

2. Your queries can combine relational data, JSON documents, and vectors.

3. All changes across your data stay in sync at all times. You don’t need to wait for them to catch up.

4. Your permissions work regardless of how you search the data and the fields you retrieve.

5. You can work with different views of the same data. For example, you can return customer data as a JSON document or relational data.

Imagine you are building an agent to manage and support tickets. For any given action, this agent would need similarity search, current ticket status, customer information, and permission checks.

With a converged database, your agent can combine all those requirements into a single query.

That means faster queries, fewer synchronization pipelines, and less coordination in your code.

Here is a really good article about converged databases:

https://t.co/rBQxsRJ03P

items.title:
💰 Passed $10M/y in revenue + investment gains this year

I've always been aggressively increasing my...
items.content:
💰 Passed $10M/y in revenue + investment gains this year

I've always been aggressively increasing my profit margins to as high as possible, especially the last few years, and especially this year where I've reduced my SaaS dependencies to just a handful of companies by vibecoding my own replacements

It's now about 94.5% profit!

Spend less -> lower costs -> more profit -> more money saved -> more money to invest -> more % returns on investments

And at some point that investment return starts to pass by your business revenue which it has for me for about a year now

Most of my investments have been simple ETFs like Vanguard S&P500, but also a few lucky stock and startup bets that worked out:

Back in 2022, I couldn't get any available GPUs, so I thought it might be smart to buy Nvidia if there's such a shortage and that was a good bet too

Then back in 2023 @dannypostma recommended me to invest in the companies we used for our AI inference for our photo AI apps, so I did that too. First I invested in @replicate and then also @FAL

From then I just asked every app/service I used if I could invest, like @cursor_ai in 2025 which then got acquired by @spacex recently!

My business revenue has remained very stable at about $200K-$250K/mo, but even with that investment returns have now surpassed that

Investments fluctuate a lot so some years it's up some years it might be down a lot (who isn't expecting a big crash at some point?), and most investment gains are unrealized (I never sell!), so keep that with a big grain of salt!

I keep my revenue/gains together with my profit margin and my sleep score in my situation monitor dashboard, as those are equally important :D

Many people in the last decade told me to spend all my money, either personally or with my business to grow it, we don't know how that would have ended up, maybe my companies would be bigger, but I'm happy I did it in my own lean profitable healthy way and it ended up great I think! 🙏😊

items.title: The pattern of underestimating AI capabilities continued when we saw virology and biosecurity expert...
items.content:
The pattern of underestimating AI capabilities continued when we saw virology and biosecurity experts and superforecasters underestimate AI-bio benchmark progress in a study we ran from late 2024 to early 2025.

The median expert forecasted that AI models would match a top virologist team on a virology troubleshooting benchmark (VCT) in 2030 while the median superforecaster thought it would take until 2034. In fact, AI models matched this baseline in April 2025, several months after the survey was conducted and 5–10 years earlier than forecasters predicted.

We also saw similar underestimation of AI progress on a cybersecurity benchmark (Cybench) in our study on LLM-enabled cybersecurity risk.

Similar underestimation occurred on the Cybench cybersecurity benchmark.

For instance, music. Apple has Dolby Atmos and has for years. 

Spotify doesn't.

But there are many other examples. 

Formula 1, for instance.

items.title: Since mid-2022, we have run 10+ major studies on AI forecasting, including expert panels on AI-bio a...
items.content:
Since mid-2022, we have run 10+ major studies on AI forecasting, including expert panels on AI-bio and AI-cyber capabilities, an adversarial collaboration between forecasters who disagree about catastrophic risk, and a Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP) focused on AI progress as a whole and the policy response to it.

These studies survey samples of highly cited and well-credentialed domain experts. Our goal was to recruit the kinds of experts that policymakers would typically turn to for advice.

For example, our initial LEAP sample included 339 total AI experts (76 computer scientists, 76 AI industry experts, 68 economists, 119 AI policy experts). Of the 76 computer scientists, 30 were professors at top-20 institutions and 10 were among the 200 top-cited authors in AI.

Our studies also include samples of forecasters with a strong track record in predicting geopolitical events (“superforecasters”).

In this analysis, we discuss how accurate forecasters have been on a subset of AI progress forecasts.

Two counterexamples ar...
items.content:
𝗛𝗼𝘄𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿, 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗱𝗼 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲 *𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴* 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗼 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗔𝗜.

Two counterexamples are:

𝟭. 𝗕𝗶𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗸-𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸𝘀

In mid-2025, in collaboration with Active Site, we asked experts to predict what fraction of STEM undergrads would be able to complete three biorisk-relevant laboratory tasks with the help of mid-2025 LLMs.

Biosecurity experts (at the median) predicted 22.5% of the sample would complete all of the tasks, virologists predicted 40%, and superforecasters predicted 16.2%.

In actuality, 5.2% of the sample could complete all of the tasks, so forecasters overestimated how much AI would help with completing these tasks.

We think it is useful to document ...
items.content:
𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘀𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗲𝘀

We think it is useful to document where typical experts under- or overestimate AI progress (and where they’re accurate). Mainstream experts often have significant power in shaping policy and public discourse, so it is useful to understand their track record on AI.

That said, we think it would be valuable to identify more accurate AI forecasts for guiding future action. So, going forward, we are prioritizing sharing several new analyses alongside standard expert panel forecasts:

1) We will share forecasts from a “fast AI progress” subsample, since this worldview has been relatively accurate at forecasting AI capabilities in recent years. We will assess where this worldview is more or less accurate in the near term.

2) We will present continuously updated forecasts from top-performing LLMs wherever possible. LLMs are reaching top human forecaster accuracy (see ForecastBench, our AI forecasting benchmark), and can quickly incorporate the most up-to-date information into regularly updated forecasts.

3) We will identify a select group of “top AI forecasters” according to their accuracy in LEAP and will highlight their forecasts as soon as we have sufficient data. An additional ~16 LEAP questions will resolve at the end of 2026, and we expect to identify a group of top forecasters in early 2027.

We’ll say more about each of these changes in a follow-up post to be published soon.

items.content:
Briefly, on potential implications of these findings:

First: if recent trends persist, most experts and forecasters are likely still underestimating how quickly AI will progress in the coming years.

Experts are already updating their views somewhat toward larger AI impacts: their predicted impact of AI by 2040 on the Technological Richter Scale (a scale devised by @NateSilver538 that ranks technologies by their broad societal impact) grew by 0.2 points on average between summer 2025 and spring 2026 (see attached figure). We will track further updates over time.

An alternative response to this evidence is to say that many of these forecasts are about relatively narrow indicators (benchmark scores, math abilities, and company revenue). Perhaps progress on these indicators will not translate into large-scale economic and societal impacts, making skeptical forecasters more accurate when it comes to forecasting AI impacts on, e.g., unemployment and economic growth.

We will continue to track accuracy on a range of AI indicators to help to adjudicate these debates.

items.content:
Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS takes the #1 spot on the Artificial Analysis Pronunciation Robustness Benchmark at 89.5%, surpassing Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS at 88.2% and SpaceXAI TTS at 87.6%

Our Pronunciation Robustness Benchmark evaluates how accurately Text to Speech models pronounce challenging text across different categories.

Key takeaways:

➤ Overall: Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS leads at 89.5%, followed by Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS at 88.2%, SpaceXAI TTS at 87.6%, and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS at 87.4%.

➤ Contextually Appropriate: Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS leads at 97.9%.

➤ Expanding Shorthand: Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS leads at 86.1%.

➤ Preserving Exact Sequences: SpaceXAI TTS retains the top spot at 85.7%.

➤ Standalone Terms: Qwen-Audio-3.0-TTS-Plus leads at 95.5%, ahead of v3 Conversational at 95.1% and Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS at 93.7%.

items.title:
Some important caveats on the above findings:

1) We discuss many questions that have resolved early...
items.content:
Some important caveats on the above findings:

1) We discuss many questions that have resolved early because AI milestones were reached sooner than expected, but this may introduce bias. By definition, we do not have data on late-resolving questions, and this may lead us to identify more areas where forecasters underestimated AI progress than where they have been accurate or overestimated progress.

2) In our analysis, for some unresolved questions we have used projections from LLMs to draw tentative accuracy conclusions. Though LLM forecasts are now comparable to strong human forecasts on many topics (see our work on ForecastBench, a forecasting benchmark), these projections are, by nature, more speculative.

We plan to continue to publish accuracy updates over time, particularly for our Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP), and will note cases where findings or projections change in a way that alters our previous interim conclusions.

items.title: Despite underestimating progress, the experts in our sample typically predict larger AI impacts and ...
items.content:
Despite underestimating progress, the experts in our sample typically predict larger AI impacts and faster progress than the general public and major government actors.

For example, the economic growth forecasts from economists in our studies were considered low by people who expect very rapid AI progress, but are meaningfully higher than comparable estimates from the IMF, OECD, and Congressional Budget Office. (See quote tweet.)

Experts also predict larger AI societal impacts as a whole than the public: the general public gives a 45% chance that AI is at least as impactful as electricity by 2040 compared to experts’ 70% chance.

Even forecasters who are very bullish on AI progress often underestimate progress.

That said, our impression is that the typical forecaster in our studies are more skeptical of AI progress than some AI observers who have more accurately predicted faster progress so far. As noted previously, we are working to address the limitations of our panel by highlighting “fast AI progress” subsamples for comparison, incorporating LLM forecasts, and identifying particularly accurate forecasters in LEAP.

Even bullish forecasters tend to underestimate AI progress.

items.title: Some argue that, although AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, diffusion of AI into the economy wi...
items.content:
Some argue that, although AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, diffusion of AI into the economy will progress much more slowly.

𝗦𝗼 𝗳𝗮𝗿, 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝘅𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝗮𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝗱𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻-𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀:

• In two of our studies, forecasters have greatly underestimated AI revenue growth, which is a relevant proxy for AI adoption. See previous tweet in this thread for an example.
• As previously noted, forecasters are on track to overestimate the rate of diffusion of self-driving cars.
• Forecasters are on track to be fairly accurate at predicting the share of electricity used for AI (3-4% by the end of 2027, against an LLM projection of 3.2%). Electricity use is one proxy for AI diffusion.

items.title: For many teams, coding is no longer the bottleneck, but you still have to decide what to build using...
items.content:
For many teams, coding is no longer the bottleneck, but you still have to decide what to build using agents.

When execution compresses to machine speed, one bottleneck that emerges is the ability to make the right decisions at the same pace.

A discussion that captures this well is "The New Cost of Product Decisions," a conversation between @TYehoshua, Chief Product & AI Officer at Atlassian, and @ElenaVerna, Head of Growth at Lovable, during the State of the AI SDLC Digital Summit.

"PMs are much more the bottleneck because when you can develop so fast, you have to pick what you're developing and make sure you're doing the right thing."

Highly suggest checking this session out.  You can watch it here:

https://t.co/Cj21HNI5pm

In addition to this session featuring Tamar & Elena, there are also sessions with leaders from Atlassian, Vercel, Honeycomb, Dropbox, 1Password, Lovable, and DX.

Thanks to the @Atlassian team for partnering with me on this post.

items.content:
.@wordgrammer says AI art should steal Adobe’s playbook: stop competing on infinite content and make Hollywood-level creation accessible to everyone.

"Adobe products took Hollywood technology and they just made it accessible to the world at large. This seemed to be a really, really good business model."

"The majority of the techniques used by influencers, by video editors, by marketers over the past 20 years have been cropping videos, editing B-roll. Significantly less time has been spent towards just taking a single 30-second long clip and making them fantastic."

"Until every single video in the world looks like Hollywood, there's no sense competing over art as if it's a scarce resource."

items.title: I couldn't find any recent and reliable comparisons of how good frontier LLMs are at coding in diffe...
items.content:
I couldn't find any recent and reliable comparisons of how good frontier LLMs are at coding in different programming languages.

I'm thinking: If I stopped reading code a year ago and don't see any issues with that, why would I still use Python as the basic language in my app? Why not switch to pure C or Rust or whatever is the fastest option these days?

But I of course am not ready to tolerate a drop in the LLM's capacity to solve problems if the language changes.

Did you see any convincing research/benchmarking of this?

We’ve collected forecasts from economists about potential AI impacts on unemployment and economic growth, but the first wave of relevant questions resolves in 2030.

In our studies, we've elicited forecasts on expected cybercrime damages, AI-enabled epidemic risk, and catastrophic risk, among other negative outcomes.

We have also elicited forecasts on major potential benefits from AI, such as improvements in life expectancy.

These are some of the most important forecasts across our work, but it's too early to say if high or low risk and benefit estimates are more accurate.

items.title: Mistral's investors saying to the brilliant trailblazers who trained Mistral and Mixtral before it w...
items.content:
Mistral's investors saying to the brilliant trailblazers who trained Mistral and Mixtral before it was cool, "Ok, stop sharing models for free and start making money. Start with OCR," are the kind of top managers that I was unlucky to work under my entire life. Most of them are like this: shortsighted career builders. Dipshits in suits.

This was the reason I resigned and am no longer employed and don't look for a job. I cannot stand working under mediocre managers. I want to smash them with something heavy each time I hear "this is not our core business" or "ROI" or some other bullshit.

I regret that the brilliant Mistral engineers and scientists haven't seen their company grow to billions in valuation and the whole world is no longer admiring the results of their work.

This kind of chance you can get only once in life, and only if you are very-very-very-...-very lucky.

This kind of chance you can get only once in life, and only if you are very-very-very-...-very lucky.

items.content:
Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS debuts at #1 in Japanese on the Artificial Analysis Controlled Voice Arena, with Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS taking the #2 spot

Our Controlled Voice Arena standardizes speaker identity across models using the same replicated reference voices, allowing us to isolate speech quality from voice preference. We evaluate models across English and 9 additional languages.

Key takeaways:

➤ Japanese: Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS takes #1 with an Elo of 1,212, followed by Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS at #2, giving Google the top two positions.

➤ Arabic and German: Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS ranks #2 in Arabic with an Elo of 1,274 and #3 in German at 1,250.

➤ Portuguese: Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS takes #2 with an Elo of 1,295.

➤ Other languages: Both models rank in the top 8 in Hindi, Spanish and French.

➤ Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS score 1,057 and 1,051 Elo, respectively, trailing Realtime TTS-2 at 1,144.

items.title: If someone had told me two years ago that I would work like this: "See the conversational reader fea...
items.content:
If someone had told me two years ago that I would work like this: "See the conversational reader feature in the web app. Create an iOS app that only has this feature and allows the user to log in and read the books in their library on their iOS app when offline. Then test the iOS app in the simulator, and once tested, submit it to the App Store." Then wait for a couple of hours and get this iOS app on my daughter's iPhone (I have an Android), I would say, "Stop bullshitting me!"

I remember last year I vibe-coded a Chrome extension for ChapterPal and then tried to do the same for Safari, and it was a bureaucratic hell, so I said, "Fuck Safari!" Now I'm thinking that I will even have an extension for Firefox, and, God forbid, Edge. And the Android app, of course, goes next with the prompt: "See the iOS app, and implement an Android app with the same features, then test it in the simulator, and publish it on Google Play Store."

If this is singularity, then the singularity is here.

Ask yes/no, multiple-choice, or scored questions and get confidence with every answer. vLLM seeds a canvas with the response template, leaves only the answer slots noisy, then reads a probability distribution from every slot in a single denoising step.

We’re launching Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS ⚡️

Our most expressive audio mod...
items.content:
We’re launching Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS ⚡️

Our most expressive audio models yet let you create custom voices across 100+ languages or pick from 2,000+ ready-to-use ones. You can direct back-and-forth conversations, guide the delivery line-by-line, and add natural cues like <laughs> or an active listening interjection like |mhm| all while generating hours of consistent, glitch-free audio.

Sounds pretty cool, right? So… how should you use them?

— Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS: Need to design bespoke vocal personas from scratch and with line-by-line level control? This is the model! Built for high-fidelity creative production like gaming, immersive audiobooks, and podcasts.

— Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS: Want the AI to automatically adjust its tone and pacing on the fly for near real-time voice agents? This is your engine! Built for cost-efficient scale, high-volume dubbing, and bulk audio creation.

items.title: One of the reasons crime numbers are going down in many places around the world and especially in Eu...
items.content:
One of the reasons crime numbers are going down in many places around the world and especially in Europe is that police simply won't let you report crimes anymore

It's clear that the big European cities are getting less safe and more run down when you visit them but you wouldn't see that from the decreasing crime statistics they publish

Yesterday I read a Dutch lawyer was sexually harassed in Amsterdam and when filing a police report, she was advised by the police not to!

Police have an incentive to show decreasing crime numbers, and they're usually underfunded so they also simply don't have the means to process so many police reports

When I visited the police station in Lisbon recently there was nobody available to help us either, or we'd have to wait for hours

Below a story from my Spanish friend who had the same in Spain!

This seems to be the case in many places now which is why we can't trust supposedly decreasing crime statistics anymore I think

items.content_html:
The Performance of Open Source Applications by Tavish Armstrong (2013) is now in @ChapterPal's collection of free books.

This book is intended for software engineers, systems architects, and advanced students who seek to design and maintain high-speed, resource-efficient applications.

It assumes a working knowledge of modern programming languages, operating system fundamentals, concurrency concepts, memory management, and standard networking protocols such as TCP/IP and HTTP.

The text focuses on the mechanics of software performance across production open-source systems, covering diverse domains including web browsers, build engines, parsers, web servers, distributed caches, test automation suites, and scientific data pipelines.

Read with an AI tutor: https://t.co/5R5aUAX0it

All books on ChapterPal are free to read with a free account.

Beautiful nature. They really love to preserve nature and the l...
items.content:
Loving my time in New Zealand 🇳🇿 ❤️

Beautiful nature. They really love to preserve nature and the local Māori culture here!

Every city in New Zealand is very well developed with good infra and quality of life everywhere, unlike in SEA countries where you see a skyscraper on one side and the other side is a big area of slums 😅

Not impressed with the food unfortunately, I miss Asian food the whole time I'm here 😂

Building a remote software company is awesome. You can travel the world and work at the same time. Not sure how much longer we have until AI take over all of the software work 😄

items.title: I can understand why Trump calls US media fake news and hates them so much. Of course, they often li...
items.content:
I can understand why Trump calls US media fake news and hates them so much. Of course, they often lie, and their coverage of the war in Ukraine is a testament to that. But one could say: this is how they cover stuff outside the US, they aren't lying about internal events to the Amertican people. Right?

Well, no. For example, yesterday Trump banned three very popular media outlets from the White House. This is outrageous; we all agree with that.

Independent media is a power, one of the four powers needed for a democracy to function (president, parliament, judges, and the press) without starting to lean toward authoritarianism when some of the four take too much power from the remaining ones.

So, what should media do when one of them is under attack? To side with them and demand to restore the status quo. They should say: attacking one of us is attacking all of us. This is the truth.

What are they saying instead? "We are fighting for the First Amendment." This is a lie and they know it. They use the "First Amendment" trigger to manipulate people's opinion, knowing that most people haven't read the Constitution, but have heard of the First Amendment and will just eat it up.

What the First Amendment actually says:

"Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances."

The important word is "Congress." Not President. Not Judge. Not Press. Congress.

So, yes, the US media are dishonest and manipulative even when they do the right thing. And they know that, and they are OK with that. This is what's disgusting.
